title: Jude and the Winter
premise: Isandro Thornbury, a substitute teacher haunted by three years of rationalized noises, discovers that every photograph from his late grandmother's house now contains an extra empty chair — and that the missing students of Hollow Creek School are being 'seated' in them. The town's oldest resident, Maren Voss, holds the papers that transfer ownership of the house, and with it the entity that demands a song be sung to keep it fed. Isandro must learn the song's forbidden last verse from Maren without ever singing along, because singing it binds the singer to the chair forever. In the end, Isandro tricks the entity into signing the papers itself, unmaking its claim to belonging, and burns the house with the last verse unfinished — freeing the children but leaving him unable to prove any of it happened.
about_author: S. M. Blackwood is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent a decade in small-town classrooms where old houses outnumbered new students. They write horror about institutions, inheritance, and the quiet violence of things that refuse to leave.

chapters.title: Substitute
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He arrives at Hollow Creek School mid-winter, replacing a teacher who 'relocated.' The classroom has thirty desks; his roster lists twenty-seven students. He notices chalk dust arranged like footprints under the floorboards. Emotional beat: wary professionalism masking an old, familiar dread.

chapters.title: The Attendance Problem
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Three students have been absent for months, yet their names appear on the register in fresh ink each morning. The principal, Mrs. Okafor, deflects with practiced ease. A custodian mutters about 'the seated ones.' Beat: unease sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: Grandma's House
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He inherits his grandmother's house on Fenwick Lane and sorts her belongings. Every family photograph — decades of them — now contains one extra empty wooden chair, always at the edge of frame. Beat: grief curdling into horror as he realizes the chair appears in photos taken before he was born.

chapters.title: The Song Overheard
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. At night he hears humming through the walls: a lullaby-like melody that stops whenever he tries to record it. His neighbor, elderly Maren Voss, warns him never to hum back. Beat: first contact with the rules of this world.

chapters.title: Empty Desk, Warm Seat
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. A fourth student stops coming. When Isandro visits the home, the parents seem foggy, insisting their daughter 'went to sit down somewhere nice.' Her bedroom chair faces the wall. Beat: the missing-class problem becomes personal.

chapters.title: Maren's Kitchen
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Maren serves tea and explains fragments: the house chooses residents, the song keeps it content, and the papers — a deed older than the county — pass ownership of both. She refuses to say what happens when no one signs. Beat: reluctant mentorship begins.

chapters.title: What the Chalk Knows
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Overnight, the classroom blackboard fills with children's handwriting: names, dates going back a century, all ending mid-sentence. One name is his grandmother's. Beat: the horror acquires genealogy; Isandro realizes his family has always been involved.

chapters.title: Three Years of Noises
chapters.summary: POV Isandro, flashback chapter. We learn why he came to Hollow Creek: three years ago, in another town, he heard something in his apartment walls and explained it away until a neighbor disappeared. Guilt drives him. Beat: character deepened; his need for justice is penance.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Classroom
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. An extra desk appears in his classroom overnight, old-fashioned, wooden, wrong. It is warm. No student claims it. Mrs. Okafor orders him to ignore it. Beat: the two hauntings — school and house — visibly converge.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Maren agrees to teach him the song, verse by verse, mouthed silently, never voiced. She demonstrates the danger: a recording of her sister, who sang along in 1968 and 'sat down' before the tape ends. Beat: stakes made visceral; training montage with dread.

chapters.title: Okafor's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He breaks into the principal's office and finds a ledger of every resident of Fenwick Lane since 1891, each entry signed and dated — and each signature followed within a year by a child's disappearance. Beat: justice outside the law theme ignites; the institution is complicit.

chapters.title: Snowbound
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. A blizzard cuts the town off. Power fails. The humming grows louder, and the extra chair appears in his own living room, facing his armchair. Beat: isolation; the entity closes distance.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Under Maren's eye, he learns the first verse — a welcome, she says, sung to make the house feel owned. That night the photographs change: the extra chair is now pulled slightly toward the table. Beat: progress with a price; the house notices him.

chapters.title: A Student Returns
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Missing student Dana reappears at school, pale, polite, reciting lessons perfectly — but she casts no breath-fog in the cold and flinches from chalk. She asks him, sweetly, if he'll come sit down sometime. Beat: hope inverted into threat.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Maren shows him the deed itself: parchment that warms to the touch, signatures crawling faintly like frost. The last living signatory is Maren herself. When she dies unsigned, the house chooses its next resident freely. Beat: deadline established — Maren's failing heart.

chapters.title: Second Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The second verse is an apology, sung to the ones already seated. Learning it, Isandro dreams of the missing children sitting in a dark dining room, waiting patiently to be remembered. Beat: compassion for the victims; resolve hardens into mission.

chapters.title: Okafor Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He confronts Mrs. Okafor with the ledger. She confesses: her predecessor's signature bound her family; keeping the school quiet keeps her son safe. She gives him a key to the school's sealed basement. Beat: antagonist revealed as fellow captive; moral complexity.

chapters.title: The Basement Classroom
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Beneath the school: a preserved one-room schoolhouse from 1891, desks arranged around a single ornate chair. On the chalkboard, the song written out in full — except the last verse, scratched away. Beat: the geography of the mystery completes; the climax's stage is set.

chapters.title: What Was Scratched Out
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Researching county archives, he finds the founding teacher, Elias Wren, who built the house and wrote the song to bind a thing that starved in winter. The last verse was meant to release it — or destroy it. Wren vanished before teaching it. Beat: lore crystallizes; the ending hinges on an unfinished act.

chapters.title: Maren Falters
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Maren suffers a stroke; in the hospital, she can mouth words but not teach. Time collapses. The humming in Isandro's house now includes voices — many, patient, hungry. Beat: ticking clock accelerates; mentor silenced at the worst moment.

chapters.title: Dana's Whisper
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Dana appears at his door at midnight and offers to teach him the last verse — the entity's offer, wearing a child's face. All he must do is sing along, just once, just quietly. Beat: temptation dramatized; he slams the door on his own longing for belonging.

chapters.title: Third Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Alone, using Maren's notes and his grandmother's letters, he reconstructs the third verse: a refusal, telling the house it owns nothing, no one. Singing it silently, he feels the photographs shift — the chair turns its back. Beat: agency reclaimed; the entity retaliates.

chapters.title: Retaliation
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The house turns hostile: doors seal, cold bites, the humming becomes screaming. His grandmother's voice joins it, begging him to sit down, rest, belong. He escapes through a window into the snow. Beat: lowest point; home itself weaponized against him.

chapters.title: The Hospital Vigil
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. At Maren's bedside, he finds her mouthing the melody over and over. A nurse mentions Maren kept singing all night — aloud. Isandro checks the visitor log: Maren's sister's name, dated 1968, signed in fresh ink. Beat: dawning horror; the entity has been collecting signatures at the hospital.

chapters.title: Okafor's Son
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Okafor's son goes missing from school. Okafor, shattered, tears up her own page of the ledger and begs Isandro to finish it, whatever it costs. Beat: ally fully converted; personal stakes doubled; the institutional cover cracks open.

chapters.title: The Seated Ones
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Following the ledger's pattern, he breaks into the sealed wing of the county poorhouse and finds the chairs — dozens, each holding a seated figure, upright, preserved, waiting. Among them, Dana. Their eyes track him. Beat: full revelation of the entity's harvest; terror and pity entwined.

chapters.title: Elias Wren's Journal
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. In the poorhouse chapel he finds Wren's journal: the last verse was never a binding but an eviction — a song that tells the house it belongs to no one, and no one to it. Wren couldn't sing it because he loved the thing too much. Beat: thematic core stated — power corrupts through love of control.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. From Wren's notation and Maren's hospital-mouthed fragments, Isandro assembles the final verse. He practices it silent, hour after hour, while the house sings his name through the walls. Beat: preparation as ordeal; discipline versus longing.

chapters.title: Maren Signs
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Dying, Maren signs the papers over to Isandro deliberately — giving him legal standing, making him the house's owner so he can evict it. Her last mouthed word: 'Finish.' Beat: passing of the torch; grief and duty fused.

chapters.title: The Summons
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The house calls him formally: every photograph in town now shows the extra chair set at his grandmother's table, place laid, waiting. Dana stands on his lawn with the whole seated congregation behind her. Beat: the entity makes its move; point of no return.

chapters.title: Into the House
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He walks into Fenwick Lane at dusk carrying the deed, the ledger, and the song. Inside, the dining room is full — every missing child, every lost resident, seated and smiling. The head chair is empty. Beat: calm-before-terror; he sits down at the table without sitting in the chair.

chapters.title: The Negotiation
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The entity speaks through the children collectively: it only wanted to belong, to be owned, to matter. It offers him everything — warmth, family, permanence. He offers it instead the papers: sign yourself away, own nothing, be free. Beat: climax of themes; power offered and refused.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The entity refuses and begins the song itself, pulling every voice including his toward the melody. Teeth gritted, throat bleeding with held-back sound, Isandro sings the last verse alone in his head — then, at the final line, aloud, solo, off-key, human. Beat: climax; the song of eviction delivered at terrible cost.

chapters.title: Eviction
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The house convulses. The chairs empty — not violently, but like sleepers waking. The entity, unowned and owning nothing, thins into the winter air, and for one moment Isandro sees it truly: small, cold, and finally unbound. Beat: catharsis; the monster pitied even in defeat.

chapters.title: Aftermath at Fenwick Lane
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Dawn. The photographs are ordinary again — grandmothers, birthdays, no extra chair. The house is just a house. He carries Maren's death notice and the burned edge of the deed to the county clerk. Beat: exhaustion and quiet grief; the supernatural recedes.

chapters.title: The Children Come Home
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. The missing students return over three days, dazed, frostbitten, alive, remembering nothing but warmth. Dana hugs him at the school gate and doesn't know why. Okafor weeps openly in the hallway. Beat: restoration; justice achieved outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Testimony Nobody Believes
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He tells the sheriff everything. There is no arrest, no report, no record — the ledger pages are blank now. He understands some wrongs can only be witnessed, not prosecuted, and decides to witness anyway. Beat: thematic resolution; justice as memory.

chapters.title: What Isandro Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. He keeps the house, lives in it, teaches through spring. Sometimes at night he almost hums the melody and stops himself. The last verse he writes down once, seals in an envelope, and does not label. Beat: bittersweet domesticity; vigilance as way of life.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: POV Isandro. Final scene: he sets a place at his table for Maren, for his grandmother, for the ones who sat too long. The chair stays empty, and that emptiness is a kind of peace. Outside, snow falls on a town that will forget. Beat: elegiac closure; belonging chosen, not taken.

chapters.title: Coda: A New Teacher Arrives
chapters.summary: POV brief third-person. Years later, a new substitute unlocks Isandro's old classroom and finds an envelope on the desk labeled only: 'If you hear humming, read this first.' She opens it. The last verse waits inside. Beat: cyclical chill; the story hands its burden to the reader.
